script.title: Why Franklin's Ships Carried Three Years of Food

lines: An explorer sailed for the Arctic with thousands of cans of food.
Between 1819 and 1822, Sir John Franklin lost 11 of the 20 men in his party.
The survivors ate lichen and even tried to eat their own leather boots.
People called him the man who ate his boots.
In 1845, Franklin led a British expedition to complete the charting of the Northwest Passage.
His ships, Erebus and Terror, carried three years' worth of preserved and tinned food.
But a cut-rate supplier won the contract only a few months before they sailed.
Sloppy solder inside the cans let lead leak into the food.
And the high heat of canning would have degraded or destroyed vitamins B1 and C.
You see, it's like living on crisps.
Your belly feels full, but your body still goes hungry.
In September 1846, the ships became trapped in ice off King William Island.
Trapped for so long, they could not hunt or escape.
The entire crew died from starvation, hypothermia and scurvy.
Because the crew carried supplies for three years, the Admiralty waited another year before searching.
In the end, more ships and men were lost looking for Franklin than in the expedition itself.

claims.claim: Between 1819 and 1822, he lost 11 of the 20 men in his party. The survivors were forced to eat lichen and even attempted to eat their own leather boots. This gained Franklin the nickname of the man who ate his boots.

The British decided to send a well-equipped Arctic expedition to complete the charting of the Northwest Passage; Franklin was named the expedition commander and the expedition set sail on 19 May 1845.
Erebus and Terror were outfitted with three years' worth of conventionally preserved or tinned preserved food supplies.

The tinned food was supplied by a cut-rate provisioner who was awarded the contract a few months before the ships were to sail; sloppily applied beads of solder on the cans' interior edges allowed lead to leach into the food.
High temperatures during canning would have degraded or destroyed vitamin B1 (thiamine) and vitamin C, both being essential to health.
Terror and Erebus became trapped in ice off King William Island in September 1846. Franklin died there on 11 June 1847.
The expedition's long entrapment was without recourse to hunting to supplement such deficiencies, or to escape.
The entire crew died from starvation, hypothermia, and scurvy.
Because the crew carried supplies for three years, the Admiralty waited another year before launching a search.
Eventually, more ships and men were lost looking for Franklin than in the expedition itself.

cast.supplier: a 40 year old London businessman, thin, a sharp narrow face, slick black hair, long black sideburns, wearing a brown and mustard checked waistcoat and a tall grey hat, 1840s
cast.sailor: a 24 year old English sailor, gaunt, curly red hair and a scruffy red beard, wearing a navy blue wool jumper and a knitted grey cap, 1840s
cast.admiral: a 66 year old Royal Navy admiral, tall and bony, bushy white eyebrows, thin white hair combed forward, wearing a black coat with broad gold braid on the cuffs, 1840s
